1:
The kindness David meant to repay is nowhere recorded, and the guesses differ. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) supposes some friendly help during the wanderings, or merely a congratulatory embassy on the accession, and makes this Nahash probably a son or grandson of the Nahash whom Saul conquered, since more than fifty years must have passed. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) takes him for the same man who had attacked Jabesh-gilead, reasoning that David had taken refuge with the Moabites next door, so that Nahash’s hatred of Saul might have induced him to befriend the fugitive. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) is less interested in the donor than in the debt: Nahash had been a cruel enemy to Israel and may have been kind only in contradiction to Saul, but if David receives kindness he is not nice in examining the grounds of it, for God knows the heart and we do not. John Gill (reformed) notes that the spoils of Ammon mentioned earlier are given by anticipation, not taken until the war now beginning.

Whether the princes’ suspicion was reasonable divides them. Henry makes it pure projection: false men are ready to think others as false as themselves, and the Ammonites would never have imagined David dissembled had they not known they could have dissembled themselves — unfounded suspicion argues a wicked mind. He borrows from Bishop Patrick that there is nothing so well meant but it may be ill interpreted by men who love nobody but themselves. Ellicott, by contrast, allows the fear some ground: Rabbah was the capital and almost the only city of the Ammonites, strongly fortified, and knowledge of its interior would matter to an enemy, while the suspicion may have been roused by David’s growing power and his conquest of the neighbouring Moabites.

On the beard they agree about the gravity and differ in how they prove it. Clarke explains that its possessor counts it his greatest ornament, often swears by it and in great matters pledges it; it was never cut but in mourning or as a sign of slavery, so halving it and the garments together made the men ridiculous, an accumulation of insult. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) supply the comparative evidence, that among the Arabs cutting off a man’s beard is reckoned an indignity quite equal to flogging and branding among ourselves and many would rather die, and they add a modern parallel in which a pretender to the Persian throne, his ambassadors’ beards cut off instead of tribute paid, came the next year with an army. Ellicott calls it the extremest insult Oriental ideas could inflict and takes the same Arab testimony over expressly from Keil. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) notes that the cutting of the garments was the worse of the two, the Israelites wearing no breeches.

Why Jericho, and in what state it stood, is the last question. Henry takes it for a private place where the men would not come into company until the shaved half had grown enough for the other to be cut to it, the Jews wearing their beards long and reckoning it an honour to appear aged and grave; change of raiment they likely had, but beards would not be so soon repaired. Keil and Delitzsch give a different reason for the halt, that David might not have to set his eyes upon the insult his servants had received. Clarke holds the town unrebuilt since Joshua, its walls unrepaired though many cottages and larger dwellings remained, and therefore comparatively private. Ellicott answers that it lay directly on their road and had been inhabited all along under the name of the city of palm trees, the curse on whoever should build it, which fell on Hiel a century later, being a curse on fortifying it rather than on dwelling there.
6:
The hired army is priced and placed, and the placing divides them. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) takes the subsidy from the parallel at a thousand talents of silver, variously estimated from a hundred and twenty-five thousand pounds to twice that, which shows the wealth of Ammon, the importance of the auxiliaries and the grave character of the war. On Beth-rehob the three part company. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) make it the capital of an Aramaean kingdom and in all probability the city named in Numbers and Judges, south of Hamath, whose position has not yet been discovered. Ellicott answers that it can hardly be that one, since that Rehob lay near Laish within Israelite territory, and prefers Rehoboth by the river, near the Euphrates, as answering to the words out of Mesopotamia in the parallel. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) puts it elsewhere again, at the extremity of the valley between Libanus and Anti-libanus, with Tob in Gilead, where Jephthah fled.

Where they mustered, and whether the lists reconcile, is Ellicott’s question. He reports from the parallel that the allies gathered at Medeba, a hill town well fitted strategically to repel an attack upon Rabbah; and he presses the discrepancy that the total of auxiliaries agrees once Maacah is left out, but the composition does not, this text naming only infantry and the other only chariots and cavalry, while the battle shows all three arms were employed — so either words have dropped from both texts or neither writer cared for details. John Gill (reformed) leaves the muster open, the Ammonites coming out either from Rabbah, as Josephus has it, or rather from Medeba on their borders.

Joab’s reading of the trap is admired by all of them, and explained differently. Clarke reconstructs it: one army was in the field and the other in the city, so that when Joab fronted the first the second issued from the gate and took him in the rear, obliging him to divide. Ellicott credits design rather than necessity: the keen eye of this experienced general took in advantage and danger at once, and he threw his force between the two divisions in two parts each able to support the other, so the enemy was cut in two while the Israelites formed one compact body. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) adds a reason for which wing Joab kept: he took the choicest men against the Syrians, whom he probably knew to be the better soldiers and, being hired men, better versed in the arts of war. The tactics succeeded: the Syrians fled, and the Ammonites, seeing the whole army of Israel free to turn on them, retired precipitately into the city.

The speech before the battle is the passage they most admire. Clarke calls it a very fine military address, equal to anything in ancient or modern times, the men fighting for hearth and altar, for God and their families and their country. Henry finds it not long but pertinent and brave, and draws from the arrangement that mutual helpfulness is brotherly duty, each to relieve the other on a signal; great dangers put an edge upon true courage, and the men were to be valiant not for pay or fame but for their people and the cities of their God. Keil and Delitzsch explain why Joab could call them so, the God of Israel having given the land to Israel as his own property, so that the brothers fought lest Jehovah’s possessions fall to the heathen and become subject to their gods. Ellicott mends the last clause, which should read not that the Lord do what seems him good but that he will do it, turning a prayer into a confession, and finds Joab’s courage rising to that highest point marked by trust that whatever the result it will be what seems best to infinite wisdom.
15:
The rally and David’s decision to lead are read together. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) makes the regathering a law of lost causes, since even the baffled cause will make head as long as there is any life in it: the Syrians called in their allies from beyond the river and hoped to make their part good, but knew not the thoughts of the Lord, who gathered them as sheaves into the floor; and David, warned of the design, would not wait to be attacked but went over Jordan at the head of his army. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reads it from the other side: Hadarezer felt the importance of his defeat and rallied all his forces, calling together even vassal tribes from beyond the Euphrates, while Joab, he suggests, was more probably employed in the south, holding the Ammonites in check and preventing a junction with their confederates.

The names give them textual work. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) notes that this Hadarezer is the Hadadezer overthrown earlier, which is the reading here of about thirty of the manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi, the two letters concerned being easily interchanged. John Gill (reformed) identifies him the same way and adds that he headed the confederacy, the rest of the kings of Syria being his servants. On Helam Ellicott is more careful: the Hebrew word need not be a proper name at all and might be rendered their host, but since the name unquestionably occurs in the next verse it is better taken as a name here too; it is omitted from the parallel, and though its situation is unknown it lay toward the Euphrates and not far from Hamath. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) attend to the general instead, reading that Shobach was so smitten that he did not survive the battle.

The casualty figures draw four methods. Clarke explains the discrepancy by scribal habit: the Jews once wrote numbers as numeral letters rather than words, and since many closely resemble each other, mistakes crept in when they came to be written out — those for seven thousand and seven hundred being such a pair, which alone would account for many numerical disagreements in these books. Ellicott decides between the readings instead, holding seven thousand chariots almost incredible and the seven hundred here evidently the more correct, while the parallel’s footmen against this text’s horsemen probably means both statements include infantry and cavalry with only one named in each. Henry simply harmonises, reading seven thousand men who belonged to seven hundred chariots, with forty thousand other soldiers, horse and foot.

Whether Hadarezer himself submitted is the sharpest division. Keil and Delitzsch grant that the first half of the verse might suggest only his vassals made peace, but hold that the closing clause, that Aram was afraid to help the Ammonites any more, shows very clearly that Hadarezer also submitted, so that the earlier expression is simply not a very exact one. Ellicott reads it the other way: it is not said that Hadarezer himself became a tributary, and a dependent of his afterwards held the territory of Damascus as an enemy of Israel, so that his submission to David and Solomon is no more than probable. Clarke observes that the vassals made peace separately and paid tribute, and reports a reading in some copies of the Vulgate and nowhere else, adding that fifty-eight thousand of them were panic-struck and fled before Israel. Henry closes on the promise that the borders of Israel should reach the Euphrates, performed at length, and on the allies, who feared to help Ammon not because the cause was unrighteous but because it had proved unsuccessful — it being dangerous to help those who have God against them, since when they fall their helpers fall with them. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) repeats both of Henry’s points in brief.
